Here is a concise, structured elaboration of the architecture and its high‑level components, their responsibilities, technologies, and interactions.

Top-level components
- UI Component (Front end)
  - Angular single-page application (TypeScript, HTML, SCSS; built to HTML/CSS/JS).
  - Runs in browser; handles rendering, client-side behaviors (sorting, validation).
  - Talks to backend over HTTP using AJAX; data format is JSON.
  - Conceptual package name ui.website (not a Java package).

- UI Server (Controllers/Servlets; part of “UI Component” server-side)
  - RESTful entry point to backend logic, implemented as Java Servlets on Google App Engine (GAE).
  - Key servlets:
    - WebPageServlet: serves initial SPA (index.html).
    - WebApiServlet: handles AJAX API calls; delegates to Action objects via ActionFactory.
    - AutomatedServlet: handles automated requests; delegates to AutomatedAction via AutomatedActionFactory.
  - Filters (e.g., OriginCheckFilter) run per web.xml order before servlets.
  - Results returned as ActionResult variants: JsonResult (common), FileDownloadResult, ImageResult.
  - Security: origin check (CSRF mitigation), authentication + authorization (GateKeeper), special bypass keys for testing (csrf/backdoor).

- Logic Component (Business logic; Java)
  - Responsibilities:
    - Business rules, relationships and cascade behavior (create/update/delete).
    - Transaction orchestration (within GAE constraints).
    - Input sanitization.
    - Access control checks (GateKeeper).
    - Integration with GAE/third-party services (task queue, email).
  - Packages:
    - logic.api: Facade and service APIs exposed to UI layer.
    - logic.core: Core domain logic.
  - Key classes:
    - Logic (Facade to multiple domain-specific logic classes and Storage).
    - GateKeeper (authorization).
    - EmailGenerator, EmailSender (pluggable provider by build config).
    - TaskQueuer (GAE task queue integration).
  - API contracts:
    - Create: null params assert; invalid -> InvalidParametersException; existing -> EntityAlreadyExistsException.
    - Retrieve: null params assert; not found -> null.
    - Update: via Attributes.UpdateOptions; not found -> EntityDoesNotExistException; invalid -> InvalidParametersException.
    - Delete: fail-delete-silently policy when target missing; cascade policies defined at Logic layer.

- Storage Component (Persistence; Java, GAE Datastore)
  - Responsibilities:
    - CRUD per entity; data validation on create/update.
    - Encapsulates datastore details and GQL queries.
    - Hides persistable entity classes (storage.entity) from other components.
    - Returns non-persistent DTOs (“Attributes”) from common.datatransfer.
    - No cascade operations; handled by Logic.
    - Addresses eventual consistency by waiting on add/delete persistence where possible (still eventual in production).
  - Packages:
    - storage.api: API used by Logic.
    - storage.entity: persistable entities (not visible outside Storage).
    - storage.search: indexing/searching support.
  - Exceptions/contracts:
    - Create: existing -> EntityAlreadyExistsException; invalid -> InvalidParametersException.
    - Retrieve: not found -> null.
    - Update: missing -> EntityDoesNotExistException; invalid -> InvalidParametersException.
    - Delete: missing -> silent.

- Common Component (Shared utilities and DTOs; Java)
  - Packages:
    - common.util: helpers/utilities.
    - common.exceptions: custom exceptions used across layers.
    - common.datatransfer: lightweight DTOs used between components (e.g., Attributes, DataBundle).
  - DTOs are often simple data structures with public fields for easy access.

- Test Driver Component (Automated regression tests; Java + Jest)
  - Purpose: component, integration, and system tests for backend; unit tests for frontend TypeScript with Jest.
  - Technologies: TestNG (Java), Jest (TS), HttpUnit (servlet-level tests without full server).
  - Packages:
    - test.driver: infra and helpers to run tests.
    - test.cases and subpackages:
      - x.testdriver, x.datatransfer, x.util, x.logic, x.storage, x.search (component tests),
      - x.webapi (system tests for user-invoked actions),
      - x.automated (system tests for automated actions).
  - Frontend tests live in *.spec.ts files.

- E2E Component (End-to-end and Load/Performance tests)
  - Black-box tests using real browsers and/or REST calls; no internal knowledge assumed.
  - Technology: Selenium (Java).
  - Packages:
    - e2e.util (helpers), e2e.pageobjects (page abstractions), e2e.cases (test cases),
    - x.util, x.e2e (system E2E tests), x.lnp (load/perf; experimental).

- Client Component (Administrative scripts)
  - Directly connects to backend for admin tasks (e.g., schema migration, statistics).
  - Packages:
    - client.util (helpers),
    - client.remoteapi (direct connection to backend),
    - client.scripts (admin operations).

Core architectural patterns and flows
- MVC mapping:
  - Model: Logic + Storage (domain, persistence).
  - View: ui.website (Angular SPA).
  - Controller: ui.controller (servlets + Action/AutomatedAction). Note: ui.website is conceptual, not a Java package.

- Template Method pattern:
  - Abstracts common request-handling flow in Action and AutomatedAction subclasses.

- Facade pattern:
  - Logic class aggregates access to domain logic and storage.

Request types and lifecycles
- User-invoked requests (99% of traffic)
  1) GAE receives request; filters apply per web.xml.
  2) Initial page load:
     - Forward to WebPageServlet -> returns index.html SPA.
     - Browser runs SPA, which issues AJAX to backend.
  3) Subsequent AJAX:
     - Forward to WebApiServlet -> ActionFactory -> Action.
     - Action: authz via GateKeeper, interact with Logic, produce ActionResult (often JSON).
     - WebApiServlet returns result to browser.
  - Static assets served directly (bypass web.xml).

- Automated requests (GAE cron and task queues)
  1) Source checked for admin privilege (403 if absent).
  2) GAE-generated requests include admin privilege; admins can trigger manually for testing.
  3) Forward to AutomatedServlet -> AutomatedActionFactory -> AutomatedAction.
  4) AutomatedAction executes using Logic as needed.
  - Config:
    - cron.xml for scheduled jobs (e.g., reminders).
    - queue.xml and Const.TaskQueue for long-running, queued tasks initiated by users but executed by GAE.

Security model
- Layered checks for Web API:
  - Origin check (CSRF mitigation).
  - Authentication and authorization via GateKeeper.
  - Bypass keys (csrf, backdoor) for controlled test/admin usage only.

Data model and transfer
- Storage entities hidden; only DTOs (“Attributes”) and other datatransfer objects flow across component boundaries.
- JSON is the primary wire format for web API and test data.
- DataBundle supports bundling arbitrary test data sets.

Operational considerations
- Environment: Google App Engine (Datastore NoSQL, Task Queue, Cron).
- Eventual consistency: mitigated for add/delete by waiting, but not fully eliminated in production distributed datastore.
- Transactions: minimized due to GAE limitations and data schema nature.

Dependencies (high-level)
- UI (browser SPA) -> UI Server (Servlets/Controllers) -> Logic (Facade, GateKeeper, services) -> Storage (Db/Datastore).
- Logic -> external services: GAE Task Queue, email provider.
- Test Driver and E2E orchestrate tests against UI Server + Logic; E2E also drives real browsers via Selenium.
- Client scripts -> Logic/Storage via Remote API for admin tasks.
- Common is a shared base for DTOs, exceptions, and utilities across all Java components.

Below is a structured elaboration of the provided BigBlueButton (BBB) architecture documentation, focusing on the high-level components, their roles, technologies, and key interactions.

High-level view (what exists and why)
- Client/UI: A browser-based HTML5 single-page app that delivers the user experience (UI, chat, whiteboard, presentations, A/V).
- Real-time collaboration core: Actor-based services that maintain meeting state and execute business logic.
- Media services: Audio conferencing and real-time media routing for webcams, screen sharing, and listen-only audio.
- API and integrations: A web application that exposes the BBB API to LMS/portals (e.g., Moodle, Greenlight) and mirrors meeting state.
- Messaging and data: Pub/Sub and state stores used for eventing, synchronization, and recording.
- Processing pipelines: Presentation conversion and recording processing.
- Edge and configuration: Reverse proxy/SSL termination plus tooling to apply configuration and manage process layout.

Client tier
- HTML5 client
  - Technology: React.js SPA, WebRTC, Meteor DDP client, MiniMongo.
  - Responsibilities:
    - Renders the UI; handles user interactions (chat, whiteboard, annotations, polls, etc.).
    - Establishes HTTPS and WebSocket connections to the BBB HTML5 server via nginx on port 443 (SSL).
    - Uses Meteor DDP to subscribe to server-published collections; receives live updates to MiniMongo.
    - Initiates/join voice via WebRTC (microphone or listen-only) and video/screen-share sessions.
- nginx
  - Responsibilities:
    - Terminates SSL on port 443 and proxies client HTTP/WebSocket traffic to the HTML5 server processes.
    - Acts as the edge entrypoint for the client.

HTML5 server (bbb-html5)
- Technology: Node.js + Meteor (ECMA2015), MongoDB.
- Responsibilities:
  - Publishes meeting-related data to clients via DDP; synchronizes client MiniMongo with server-state in MongoDB.
  - Handles client requests/events, forwards/receives events to/from back-end services (via Redis PubSub and bbb-web/akka apps).
  - Manages per-meeting queues triggered by MeetingStarted/MeetingEnded events.
- Scalability model (2.3+):
  - Multiple Node.js processes: separate “frontend” and “backend” processes (default: 2 each; configurable).
  - Frontend roles:
    - Complete authentication via ValidateAuthTokenResp.
    - Collect client subscriptions/publishers; receive DDP events/method calls and route to akka apps.
    - Handle Streamer-related Redis events (Cursor, Annotations, External video share).
    - Create/destroy per-meeting processing queues on MeetingStarted/MeetingEnded.
  - Backend roles:
    - Process all non-streamer events.
    - If multiple backends run, bbb-web assigns instanceId (round-robin) so each backend handles a subset of meetings.
    - Also receives ValidateAuthTokenResp when operating without frontends (e.g., dev).
  - Configuration/runtime:
    - Managed via bbb-conf; apply-config.sh runs between shutdown/restart to apply config changes.

API and integration tier
- BBB Web (bbb-web)
  - Technology: Java-based application written in Scala (Akka ecosystem alignment).
  - Responsibilities:
    - Implements the BBB API used by third-party front-ends (Moodle, Canvas, Sakai, WordPress, Greenlight).
    - Maintains a copy of meeting state; orchestrates meeting lifecycle.
    - Balances backend processing by assigning instanceId to bbb-html5 backends (round-robin).
  - Integrations:
    - All external access goes through a front-end portal calling the BBB API.
    - Greenlight is the default reference front-end; API demos included.

Real-time collaboration core
- Apps Akka
  - Technology: Akka (actor model).
  - Responsibilities:
    - Main application orchestrating real-time meeting features: users list, chat, whiteboard, presentations.
    - MeetingActor contains the meeting business logic and state; processes all meeting messages.
- FSESL Akka
  - Responsibilities:
    - Isolates the FreeSWITCH integration into a dedicated application.
    - Communicates with FreeSWITCH via Event Socket Layer (ESL) using Redis PubSub for message exchange.
    - Enables alternative voice backends to be integrated by replacing this component.

Media services
- FreeSWITCH
  - Responsibilities:
    - Core voice conferencing engine (headset-based join via WebRTC; PSTN/VOIP call-in integration possible).
    - Provides high-quality, low-latency audio for participants; integrates with WebRTC-capable browsers.
- Kurento Media Server (KMS) and WebRTC-SFU
  - Responsibilities:
    - KMS streams webcams, listen-only audio, and screen sharing.
    - The WebRTC-SFU acts as the media controller to negotiate and manage media streams.

Messaging and data
- Redis PubSub
  - Responsibilities:
    - Event bus for inter-process communication among BBB applications (bbb-web, Apps Akka, FSESL, bbb-html5).
    - Transports events like annotations, cursor updates, external video share, meeting lifecycle, etc.
- Redis DB
  - Responsibilities:
    - Persistent store for recorded events during a meeting.
    - Feeds the Recording Processor with events and raw media (PDF, WAV, FLV) after the meeting ends.
- MongoDB
  - Responsibilities:
    - Stores the live state referenced by the HTML5 server and clients.
    - Server publishes collections; client-side MiniMongo auto-updates via DDP.

Processing pipelines
- Recording Processor
  - Responsibilities:
    - After meeting ends, processes recorded events and raw files into final recording artifacts.
- Presentation conversion
  - Flow:
    - Upload → if Office doc, convert to PDF via LibreOffice → convert to SVG via bbb-web.
    - Progress updates sent to clients through Redis PubSub.
    - Fallback logic: if SVGs are too heavy, rasterized images are embedded in SVG to improve client performance.
  - Configurable conversion targets: SWF, SVG, PNG (enable/disable).

Key user flows
- Joining a voice conference
  - From HTML5 client: user chooses Microphone or Listen Only; client sets up a WebRTC connection.
  - FreeSWITCH provides the voice conference; WebRTC affords low-latency, high-quality audio.
  - Listen-only audio is streamed by KMS (integrated into the overall media plane).
- Streaming video and screensharing
  - KMS handles the media; WebRTC-SFU manages stream negotiation/control.
- Uploading a presentation
  - Client uploads; conversion pipeline runs; updates are published over Redis; finalized assets are served to clients.

Configuration and lifecycle
- bbb-conf and apply-config
  - bbb-conf --setip or --restart triggers apply-config.sh between shutdown/restart.
  - Allows centralized, scripted application of config changes (via helper functions in apply-lib.sh).
  - Changes to bbb-html5 roles/process counts require a restart.

Connectivity summary
- External client connectivity:
  - HTTPS and WebSocket to nginx on port 443 (SSL), proxied to HTML5 server.
- Internal connectivity:
  - Services communicate via sockets with Redis PubSub as the core event bus and MongoDB for state sync.
  - Media paths are established via WebRTC to FreeSWITCH and KMS/SFU.

High-level components to carry forward
- Client/UI: HTML5 client (React, WebRTC, MiniMongo).
- Edge: nginx reverse proxy/SSL terminator.
- HTML5 server: Meteor/Node services with frontend/backend roles; MongoDB for live state.
- API/integration: BBB Web (Scala/Java) exposing the BBB API; Greenlight and LMS plugins as clients.
- Real-time core: Apps Akka (MeetingActor and related actors) for meeting logic.
- Voice integration: FSESL Akka bridging to FreeSWITCH (ESL) via Redis.
- Media: FreeSWITCH (voice), Kurento Media Server + WebRTC-SFU (webcams, screensharing, listen-only).
- Messaging/data: Redis PubSub (events), Redis DB (recording events), MongoDB (client/server state).
- Processing: Recording Processor; Presentation Conversion pipeline (LibreOffice → PDF → SVG/PNG fallback).
- Ops/config: bbb-conf, apply-config.sh, role/process configuration for scalability.

Here is a clear, high-level breakdown of the Media Store architecture described, with components, responsibilities, and their main interactions.

Top-level view (tiers and core responsibilities)
- Presentation tier
  - Facade: Server-side web front end. Delivers pages (registration, login, browse/list, upload, download), manages user sessions, collects user input, initiates application use cases, and streams responses/files to users.
- Application/business tier
  - MediaManagement: Central orchestration/business logic. Coordinates user requests across other components (metadata, storage, re-encoding, watermarking, packaging).
  - UserManagement: Handles user registration and authentication. Implements password salting and hashing.
- Integration/services tier
  - MediaAccess: Gateway for audio content and its metadata. Encapsulates DB access for audio metadata and handles storing/fetching audio files to/from file storage.
  - UserDBAdapter: Gateway for user data. Encapsulates DB access for user accounts and password hashes.
  - ReEncoder: Converts audio bitrates (transcoding) for downloads to reduce size or enforce distribution profile.
  - TagWatermarking: Applies a unique, per-user digital watermark to downloaded files after re-encoding.
  - Packaging: Archives multiple files for bulk download (e.g., zip).
- Persistence tier
  - Database: Relational DB (e.g., MySQL). Stores user accounts, salted password hashes, and audio metadata (e.g., name, genre).
  - DataStorage: File storage for actual audio files (separate from the DB; could be a dedicated file server or local disk).

Component details and boundaries
- Facade
  - Provides: Web pages and APIs for registration, login, listing, browsing, upload, download; session management; streaming of completed files to users.
  - Requires: UserManagement (for auth), MediaManagement (for all media-related operations).
- MediaManagement
  - Provides: Application use-case orchestration (list, upload, download single/multi).
  - Coordinates: MediaAccess (metadata and file I/O), ReEncoder, TagWatermarking, Packaging; interacts with DataStorage via MediaAccess.
  - Note: The text says MediaManagement “fetches audio files from a specific location,” but elsewhere MediaAccess is responsible for storage I/O. Treat MediaManagement as orchestrator that delegates actual I/O to MediaAccess.
- UserManagement
  - Provides: Registration, authentication, password hashing + salting.
  - Requires: UserDBAdapter for DB CRUD on users and password hashes.
- MediaAccess
  - Provides: Encapsulated operations for audio metadata (DB) and file I/O (DataStorage).
  - Responsibilities:
    - List available audio files (via Database).
    - Store uploaded files (to DataStorage) and persist metadata (to Database).
    - Retrieve metadata for download and coordinate file retrieval from DataStorage.
  - Note: The text mentions “AudioAccess” once when listing files; treat it as a naming slip for MediaAccess.
- UserDBAdapter
  - Provides: Encapsulated DB access for user data (create user, lookup by username/email, verify credentials via retrieved salted hash).
- ReEncoder
  - Provides: Bitrate conversion/transcoding used during download (not during upload).
- TagWatermarking
  - Provides: Applies a per-user digital watermark to re-encoded files; ensures downloaded files are uniquely tied to a user ID for traceability.
- Packaging
  - Provides: Archive creation for multi-file downloads (e.g., zip/tar.gz).
- Database
  - Stores: User info, salted password hashes, and audio metadata.
- DataStorage
  - Stores: Actual audio file binaries; decoupled from Database.

Key interactions (typical flows)
- Registration
  - Facade -> UserManagement -> UserDBAdapter -> Database (store user with salted+hashed password) -> Facade (session start or login prompt).
- Login
  - Facade -> UserManagement -> UserDBAdapter -> Database (retrieve salted hash) -> UserManagement (verify) -> Facade (establish session).
- List/browse audio
  - Facade -> MediaManagement -> MediaAccess -> Database (fetch metadata list) -> MediaManagement -> Facade (render list).
- Upload audio
  - Facade (receives file) -> MediaManagement -> MediaAccess
    - MediaAccess -> DataStorage (store file)
    - MediaAccess -> Database (store metadata)
  - MediaManagement -> Facade (acknowledge). Note: no re-encoding or watermarking on upload.
- Download a single file
  - Facade -> MediaManagement
    - MediaManagement -> MediaAccess -> Database (fetch metadata)
    - MediaManagement -> MediaAccess -> DataStorage (retrieve original file)
    - MediaManagement -> ReEncoder (transcode/re-bitrate as required)
    - MediaManagement -> TagWatermarking (embed user-specific watermark)
  - MediaManagement -> Facade (stream watermarked file to user).
- Download multiple files
  - Repeat the single-file process for each selection (metadata, fetch, re-encode, watermark)
  - MediaManagement -> Packaging (archive bundle)
  - MediaManagement -> Facade (stream the archive).

Non-functional concerns addressed by the design
- Security: Salted+hashed passwords; session management; per-user watermarking deters and traces redistribution.
- Separation of concerns: Clear split between presentation, business/orchestration, integration (adapters/services), and persistence.
- Scalability/extensibility:
  - Decoupling DB and file storage enables independent scaling and varied storage backends.
  - Media processing components (ReEncoder, TagWatermarking, Packaging) are isolated and can be scaled horizontally.
- Performance considerations:
  - Re-encoding and watermarking occur on download, which may be CPU-intensive; batching + Packaging reduces client round-trips.

Clarifications and assumptions
- “AudioAccess” is assumed to be the same as “MediaAccess.”
- When the text says MediaManagement “fetches audio files,” it is interpreted as orchestration; MediaAccess performs actual file I/O.
- Database holds only metadata and user data; binary audio files live exclusively in DataStorage.

List of identified high-level components
- Facade (web front end + sessions)
- MediaManagement (business orchestration)
- UserManagement (registration/auth + hashing/salting)
- MediaAccess (audio metadata + file storage access)
- UserDBAdapter (user data access)
- ReEncoder (transcoding)
- TagWatermarking (per-user watermarking)
- Packaging (bulk archive)
- Database (relational store for users and metadata)
- DataStorage (file server/local disk for audio content)

Here’s an elaboration of the provided TeaStore architecture, focusing on the high-level components, their responsibilities, interactions, data flows, and key design choices.

High-level components (5 replicable services + 1 single-instance registry)
- WebUI (replicable)
- Image Provider (replicable)
- Auth Service (replicable)
- Persistence Provider (replicable)
- Recommender (replicable)
- Registry (single instance per TeaStore deployment)

System overview
- WebUI is the front-end server (Servlets + JSP) that orchestrates calls to backend services, manages cookies/sessions, and renders pages.
- Image Provider serves images as base64 strings for embedding, with on-demand scaling and LFU caching.
- Auth handles user authentication and session validation with secure hashing.
- Persistence Provider abstracts the relational database via JPA (EclipseLink), exposing CRUD APIs and leveraging a second-level cache.
- Recommender generates personalized product recommendations using multiple algorithms.
- Registry maintains live service instance metadata, performs lightweight health via heartbeat, and enables the UI status page.

Responsibilities and key behaviors per component
1) WebUI
- Renders HTML pages via Servlets and JSP.
- Orchestrates data fetching:
  - Product/catalog/cart/order data from Persistence Provider.
  - Recommendations from Recommender.
  - Images from Image Provider (as base64).
  - Authentication/session checks via Auth.
- Cookie management (stores/retrieves values; includes session-related cookie).
- Status page:
  - Queries Registry to list all registered service instances (hosts and counts).
- Design note: Images are mostly delegated to Image Provider to offload image handling and caching.

2) Image Provider
- Input: product ID or UI name (for non-product images) and desired size.
- Behavior:
  - If ID/name missing: return a standard “not found” image in requested size.
  - If ID/name exists but size missing: load largest available image, scale down, deliver and persist the scaled variant for future reuse.
  - If exact ID/name and size exist: deliver directly.
- Performance:
  - In-memory LFU cache used to accelerate delivery; lookup before disk access.
  - Delivers base64-encoded image for direct embedding in HTML produced by WebUI.
- State:
  - On-disk image store (originals).
  - In-memory cache (per instance).
  - Persisted scaled images stored for reuse.

3) Auth Service
- User authentication:
  - Passwords hashed with BCrypt (slow hash for security).
- Session validation:
  - SessionBlob salted and hashed with SHA-512; hash stored in a cookie.
  - Upon request, re-salts and verifies hash to detect tampering.
- Interacts with WebUI for login, session checks, and logout flows.
- Security note: Cookie integrity is ensured via hashing; confidentiality requires transport security (TLS) and secure cookie flags (not specified but recommended).

4) Persistence Provider
- Data access layer for the relational database.
- Exposes CRUD endpoints for all persistent entities (e.g., products, users, orders, carts).
- Uses EclipseLink JPA ORM to map between relational entities and JSON objects exchanged between services.
- Second-level cache (JPA) acts as an application-level caching layer to reduce DB load.
- State: Backed by a relational DB; cache is per-instance (not shared).

5) Recommender
- Generates recommendations using:
  - Fallback: global popularity (for unknown users).
  - Slope One item-based collaborative filtering:
    - CPU-intensive online scoring variant.
    - Memory-intensive precomputed user-item prediction matrix variant.
  - Order-based nearest-neighbor approach:
    - Latency proportional to current cart size and total orders.
- Training data source: historical orders (from Persistence).
- Output influenced by:
  - Current cart contents.
  - User’s past orders.
  - Currently viewed item.

6) Registry (single instance)
- Tracks live instances of each service:
  - Services register at startup and renew registration as a heartbeat.
  - Missed heartbeat > 10s marks instance as offline until it re-registers.
- Used by WebUI’s status page to display instance counts and hosts.
- Deployment note: Single instance simplifies multi-TeaStore setups but is a single point of failure for service discovery/status.

Data flows and typical interactions
- Page render (e.g., product page):
  1) WebUI validates session with Auth (via session cookie).
  2) WebUI queries Persistence for product data.
  3) WebUI fetches related images from Image Provider (product ID + desired sizes).
  4) WebUI requests recommendations from Recommender (current user/cart/item).
  5) WebUI renders HTML with embedded base64 images.
- Login:
  1) WebUI sends credentials to Auth.
  2) Auth verifies BCrypt password hash.
  3) WebUI receives a SessionBlob-derived cookie (salted+SHA-512 hash) and stores it.
- Image request handling in Image Provider:
  1) Check in-memory LFU cache for requested ID/name + size.
  2) On miss: check disk; if size missing, load largest, scale, store scaled image, update cache.
  3) Return base64.
- Training recommender:
  - Recommender fetches historical orders from Persistence, trains selected model variant, then serves predictions.

Scalability and state
- Replicable services: WebUI, Image Provider, Auth, Persistence Provider, Recommender.
- Stateless vs stateful considerations:
  - WebUI: mainly stateless; session state held in cookies. Some transient state (cookie handling).
  - Image Provider: per-instance in-memory LFU cache; scaled images persisted (shared store assumed).
  - Persistence Provider: per-instance JPA second-level cache; backed by shared relational DB.
  - Recommender: model state in memory or persisted depending on implementation; training frequency/strategy impacts memory and startup times.
  - Auth: state mainly in DB and cookies; stateless verification logic.
- Registry is single-instance; all services depend on it for registration/visibility.

Performance and reliability
- Caching layers:
  - Image Provider LFU cache for hot images.
  - Persisted scaled images to avoid repeated transforms.
  - JPA second-level cache to reduce DB round-trips.
- Fault handling:
  - Missing images: serves standard placeholder.
  - Registry heartbeat: instances marked offline after 10s gap.
- Potential bottlenecks/single points:
  - Single Registry instance.
  - Recommender training or online inference variant could be CPU/memory intensive.
  - Image scaling spikes on cache cold starts.
- Latency considerations:
  - WebUI makes multiple downstream calls per page; network hop count can influence response times.
  - Base64 images increase payload size but reduce additional image fetches by the browser.

Security considerations
- Passwords: BCrypt hashing (good for brute-force resistance).
- Session integrity: SHA-512 salted hash in cookie prevents tampering; ensure secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies and TLS.
- Service-to-service communication should use TLS and authentication (not specified; recommended).

Operations and observability
- Status page in WebUI reflects Registry data: instance counts and hosts per service.
- Heartbeat re-registration provides basic liveness info.
- Recommender model lifecycle (training schedule, warmup) should be monitored.

Assumed technologies/protocols (implied by description)
- HTTP/REST with JSON between services.
- JSP/Servlets for UI.
- EclipseLink JPA with a relational database.
- Base64 image embedding.

Summary mapping of responsibilities
- WebUI: Presentation, orchestration, cookies, status page.
- Image Provider: Image lookup, scaling, LFU caching, base64 delivery.

Here is a concise elaboration that identifies the high-level components, their responsibilities, and the dependency/interaction rules implied by the documentation.

High-level architectural style
- Layered/onion-style architecture: model at the center, logic around it, user interfaces as the outer shell. All dependencies point inward toward the center.

Core components and responsibilities
1) Model (domain core)
- What it is: The canonical data model and domain events.
- Key types: BibDatabase(s), BibEntry(ies), Events, and related value objects/entities.
- Responsibility: Represent domain state and basic invariants; only minimal logic that is intrinsic to the data itself.
- Dependency rule: No dependencies on other JabRef classes or layers. Pure domain.

2) Logic (application/services layer)
- What it is: Application logic and operations over the model.
- Responsibility: Read/write/import/export, manipulate model objects, enforce application workflows; expose APIs used by UIs.
- Dependency rule: Depends only on the Model. No knowledge of UI or user preferences.

3) GUI (graphical user interface)
- What it is: Desktop/presentation layer.
- Responsibility: Interact with the user, mediate user intents to Logic, render model state, manage user preferences, and orchestrate workflows using the Logic API.
- Dependency rule: May depend on Logic and Model (inward), but not vice versa.

4) CLI (command-line interface)
- What it is: Alternative presentation layer.
- Responsibility: Provide command-line access to application capabilities by calling Logic APIs; parse CLI arguments, report results.
- Dependency rule: Depends on Logic and Model (inward). Treated as an outer layer like GUI.

5) Preferences (user configuration)
- What it is: Utility package for user-customizable settings.
- Responsibility: Represent and persist user-specific configuration.
- Dependency rule: Consumed by presentation layers (GUI, and possibly CLI if needed). Core layers (Logic, Model) must not depend on Preferences; any needed settings are passed in from the outer layers.

6) Event bus (infrastructure for decoupled notifications)
- What it is: Publish/subscribe mechanism.
- Responsibility: Model publishes events; outer layers (Logic if acting as an orchestrator, GUI/CLI) subscribe to react to changes without violating dependency direction.
- Dependency rule: Events originate in the Model; subscriptions occur in outer layers. This preserves inward-only compile-time dependencies while enabling outward reactions at runtime.

Architecture guardrails and packaging
- Dependency direction: Only inward toward the Model. No outward or lateral dependencies across peer layers.
- Vertical structuring: Within each layer, packages are formed by responsibility (feature verticals) rather than by purely technical concerns.
- Enforced by tests: JUnit architectural tests verify critical dependency constraints (Model ↔ Logic ↔ GUI), failing the build on violations.

Typical interaction flows
- User flow (GUI): User action -> GUI uses Preferences as needed -> GUI calls Logic API -> Logic manipulates Model -> Model emits Events -> GUI reacts via event bus to update views.
- Batch/CLI flow: Command execution -> CLI calls Logic API -> Logic manipulates Model -> Model emits Events -> CLI may react/log results.

Key rules to preserve
- Model is pure and independent.
- Logic depends only on Model; presented as an API for UIs.
- Presentation layers (GUI/CLI) own user interaction and any preference usage.
- Event bus enables reacting to model changes without breaking dependency direction.

Resulting qualities
- Clear separation of concerns, testability, and maintainability.
- Stable domain center with constrained coupling.
- Flexible UI layers (GUI/CLI) built on a consistent Logic API.
- Architectural integrity enforced continuously by tests.
